jati: Sampurna-Sampurna (7 notes, though all komal variants are used freely)
time_of_day: Morning; also sung at end of any concert regardless of time
aaroh: Sa re ga Ma Pa dha ni Sa
avaroh: Sa ni dha Pa Ma ga re Sa
notes_used: Re komal, Ga komal, Ma shuddh, Dha komal, Ni komal — all four komal notes
characteristic_pakad: Ma ga re Sa, ni dha Pa, Ma ga re Sa
emotional_resonance: feeling unvalued by someone you love — husband, partner, family
longing for something that is gone
feeling like love was not returned
after a painful argument with someone close
when leaving home or a place you love
therapy_note: Bhairavi is the raag of compassion — it holds grief without drowning in it. All four of its komal (flat) notes create a sound that is simultaneously tender and vast. It is traditionally sung last at concerts because it is believed to bring a performance to the deepest emotional completion — it touches grief but resolves it gently. Unlike Todi which is inward and searching, Bhairavi is outward and accepting. It is the musical equivalent of being held while you cry.

classical_reference: Sung by virtually every major Hindustani vocalist. Farewell raag of all concerts. Pandit Bhimsen Joshi's 'Raga Bhairavi' and Kishori Amonkar's recordings are legendary. Bandish: 'Baaje Re Muraliya Baaje'
notes_for_vocalist: In Bhairavi, all four komal notes (re, ga, dha, ni) must be sung with full weight — do not soften them further or sharpen them accidentally. Bhairavi also permits the use of all 12 notes as ornaments (gamaks and meends) — this is unique to Bhairavi. Ma is the vadi and must be rested upon. The aalaap should be slow, contemplative, and without hurry. This raag should never be rushed.
